source_refs.note: Topic 7.4.4, printed pages 157-158, with Quick Check 7.7 as the self-check.

blocks.text: The rate constant is specific for a particular reaction at a certain temperature. Since concentrations are in mol dm-3 and rate in mol dm-3 s-1, the units of k depend on the order of the reaction and the unit of time. From rate = k [reactants]^n, k = rate / [reactants]^n = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^n, so k = (mol dm-3)^(1-n) s-1, or k = (concentration)^(1-n) s-1, which gives the units for any order.

blocks.prompt: A rate constant is 3.5 x 10^-4 s-1 at 25 degrees C. What is the order of the reaction, what is the initial rate when the reactant is 0.50 mol dm-3, and what happens to the rate if the concentration is doubled? Why do chemists want the order and the rate constant?
blocks.explanation: Units of s-1 mean first order. Initial rate = k [A] = 3.5 x 10^-4 x 0.50 = 1.75 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 s-1. Doubling the concentration doubles the rate. Knowing the order and k lets a chemist predict the rate under any concentrations, choose economic conditions for a process, and deduce the mechanism, which the balanced equation alone cannot give.

items: k = (mol dm-3)^(1-n) s-1: zero order mol dm-3 s-1, first order s-1, second order dm3 mol-1 s-1, third order dm6 mol-2 s-1; the units of k reveal the order.
